Neonatal Red deer calves are surprisingly robust, with newborn individuals typically weighing around 10,100 grams [Wwb = around 10,100 grams], a substantial birth mass that reflects the species' strategy of producing a single, precocial offspring capable of following its mother within hours of parturition. This considerable initial investment is followed by a period of rapid growth sustained entirely through maternal milk. Under the stable core body temperature characteristic of this large ungulate, measured at 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], the interval from parturition to weaning is relatively brief for an animal of this size; calves achieve nutritional independence from milk approximately 156 days after birth [tx = approximately 156 days after birth], by which point they have grown to a wet weight at weaning of approximately 56,500 grams [Wwx = approximately 56,500 grams]. This relatively early weaning age, recorded in a study of a Scottish highland population, allows the hinds to regain body condition before the autumn rutting season. The abrupt transition from a milk-based diet to solid forage, typically grass and herbaceous plants, represents a critical developmental hurdle. Mortality during this weaning period can be high, particularly among calves born late in the spring who have less time to accumulate sufficient fat reserves before winter, a seasonal bottleneck that exerts strong selective pressure on birth timing within the population.

Adult body mass in Red deer exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a feature common among polygynous cervids. Mature females, or hinds, typically attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 150,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 150,000 grams] in prime condition, though individuals in particularly productive habitats can exceed 170 kilograms. Stags, by contrast, reach a far greater ultimate wet weight of roughly 230,000 grams [Wwi = roughly 230,000 grams], a size advantage that is essential for success in the intense male-male combat that characterizes the species' breeding system. This dramatic difference in body mass is not fully expressed until well after sexual maturity, as young males continue somatic growth for several years after females have reached their asymptotic size. The energetic demands of maintaining such a large body, particularly the cost of growing and carrying a heavy set of antlers each year, constrain the maximum recordable lifespan. These weight values, derived from a long-term study of the Isle of Rum population, are considered representative of the species across its European range, although some continental populations show consistently heavier average masses, likely reflecting differences in forage quality and growing season length.

Reproduction in Red deer is tightly linked to seasonal cycles and maternal body condition. The gestation period, a remarkably consistent trait across populations, lasts approximately 245 days [tg = approximately 245 days] at the species' normal internal body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], which aligns with the typical range of 240 to 262 days reported in the literature. This lengthy pregnancy is timed so that parturition coincides with the spring flush of vegetation, maximizing the availability of high-quality forage for the lactating hind. An individual hind typically produces a single calf per litter [N_R_i = single calf per litter], with a reproductive frequency of approximately 1 litter per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 litter per year], with twin births being exceptionally rare in most populations. This low annual fecundity is offset by a long potential reproductive lifespan; hinds that survive their first few years can produce calves annually for a decade or more. The success of any given reproductive event is heavily influenced by the hind's nutritional status entering the winter, as poor body condition can lead to early embryonic loss or the birth of a weak, low-birth-weight calf that fails to survive its first summer.

The timing of key life-history transitions in Red deer is strongly influenced by the nutritional environment and social factors. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of this large cervid (38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]), puberty is attained relatively late, with individuals reaching sexual maturity at approximately 852 days after birth [tp = approximately 852 days after birth]. This translates to an age at first potential reproduction of roughly 2.3 years, though in practice, most females do not successfully breed until their third year of life, and males rarely achieve reproductive success before they are at least five years old due to the hierarchical social structure. The delay in male reproduction is not due to a lack of physiological maturity, but rather their inability to compete with older, larger stags for access to oestrous hinds during the rut. This deferred age at first reproduction for males is a classic example of how social constraints can decouple physiological readiness from actual reproductive output. A young stag may be capable of siring offspring long before he has the body mass and antler size necessary to hold a harem.

Maximum longevity in Red deer is considerable for a terrestrial mammal of its size, with the oldest documented individuals surviving to approximately 11,500 days [am = approximately 11,500 days] under the standard body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to around 31.5 years, is most commonly recorded in well-studied, protected populations on islands where predation is absent and human hunting pressure is minimal. In mainland populations subject to wolf or bear predation, or to managed culling, the average lifespan is far shorter, and very few individuals reach such an advanced age. The senescence pattern in this species is notable for its gradual nature; unlike some ungulates that experience a sharp decline, Red deer hinds can remain reproductively active well into their late teens and early twenties, though calf survival rates from older mothers tend to decline. The trade-off between longevity and high annual reproductive effort is evident when comparing population densities: hinds on poor-quality ranges live longer on average but produce fewer calves over their lifetime than those on richer ranges where higher immediate reproductive output is possible.
